subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 15 periods = 600 minutes
Total: 15 periods · 10h 0min

periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Look at the map for the southernmost point of India (p. 95)
materials: political map of India (wall map or printed)
periods.visual_aids: Political/physical map of India showing island territories

time_bands.activity: Teacher places the wall map of India in view and asks students to find where India ends in the south. Students share their ideas aloud before opening their textbooks.

Students open Textbook p. 95 and examine the map to locate Indira Point, the southernmost tip of India. They identify the sea around the Andaman and Nicobar Islands and note other island groups visible on the map. Students record in their notebooks: the name of the southernmost point, the sea in which the islands lie, and any other island names they can find.

Class shares findings. Teacher scribes responses on the board under two columns: 'What the map shows' and 'What we already knew.' Students add any islands they know from their own experience or from stories, completing the task on Textbook p. 95.

Students write two observations in their notebook: one about where India's islands are located and one about why they think islands might feel different from the mainland. Teacher circulates, prompting with 'What do you notice about the colour of the sea around them?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate and name natural geographic features using map symbols and spatial position.
periods.section_context: Indira Point as southernmost tip of India, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Bay of Bengal, other Indian island groups visible on the map.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'If you were standing on an island, what would you see in every direction?' This opens the definition of an island organically. Prompt quieter students by asking what colour surrounds the island on the map.

periods.activity_title: Buttress Root Model — Building for Stability
periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Roll newspaper into a tube, stand it up, add triangular supports, test stability (p. 96)
materials: thick paper or card for triangles
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of buttress roots on p. 96

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the textbook image of buttress roots on p. 96 without naming them. Students describe what they see: 'What shape are those root structures? What are they doing for the tree?'

Students follow the activity on Textbook p. 96: roll a sheet of newspaper into a thin tube and glue the edge. They stand it on the desk and observe whether it stays upright. Students record their observation in one sentence. They then cut three or four small triangles from thick paper, attach them evenly around the base, and stand the tube again. They record the second observation.

Groups share results. Teacher connects the triangle supports to buttress roots: 'The triangles do the same job as those wide root flanges — they spread the load so the tall tree doesn't fall.' Students sketch the tube with and without supports and label the sketch 'without supports' and 'with supports.'

Students write a one-sentence conclusion in their notebook answering: 'What does a wide base do for a tall structure?' Teacher asks which other tall things around us need a wide base to stay standing, drawing out examples from students' own environment.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple structural model to infer the engineering principle that a wider base increases the stability of a tall structure.
periods.section_context: Paper-tube model without base support, triangular paper supports as buttress-root analogues, stability test on flat surface.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What changed between the first and second test — only one thing changed. What was it?' This keeps the inquiry clean and helps students identify the variable. Groups of three work well for this build-and-test task.

periods.activity_title: Life Under the Sea — Coral Reefs and Marine Creatures
periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Why do you think life under the sea is just as important as life in the forests? (p. 98)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of coral reef and marine life on pp. 97–98

time_bands.activity: Students list at least three living things found in the sea in their notebooks (Textbook p. 98). Teacher asks a few students to share, building a class list on the board. Students add any creatures from the list they had not thought of.

Teacher reads aloud the description of the Marine Interpretation Centre and coral reefs from the textbook (pp. 97–98). Students look at the illustrations and identify creatures they can name. Discussion prompt: 'How do you think the coral reef helps the fish and other sea creatures?' Students share ideas in pairs before opening to the whole class.

Class discussion: 'Why do you think life under the sea is just as important as life in the forests?' (Textbook p. 98.) Teacher guides students to draw parallels between forest canopy layers and coral reef layers as shelters. Students also discuss the drawing or writing task about their favourite sea animal (Textbook p. 97) and complete a quick sketch or written sentence in their notebook.

Students write two sentences: one naming a coral reef creature and the role the reef plays for it, and one connecting sea life to forest life using the comparison from discussion. Teacher closes by asking: 'What would happen to the reef creatures if the coral disappeared?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the role of a natural habitat structure in sheltering living things and explain why aquatic ecosystems matter alongside land ecosystems.
periods.section_context: Coral reefs, Marine Interpretation Centre, Andaman sea creatures including fish, marine invertebrates; parallel between reef shelter and forest shelter.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Draw out students' personal connections: 'Has anyone seen fish in a tank, pond, or river? How does the tank or weed in the water help the fish?' Moving from familiar to unfamiliar keeps the discussion grounded.

periods.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — How do you think their knowledge might have helped the people of North Sentinel Island stay safe? (p. 98)

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly describes the North Sentinel Island community — a people who live by deep knowledge of the forest, sea, and sky — without giving away the tsunami connection. Students are asked: 'What kinds of things would you need to know about your surroundings to stay safe there?'

Students read or listen to the relevant passage in the textbook about North Sentinel Island and the 2004 tsunami (p. 98). Discussion: 'How do you think their knowledge might have helped the people of North Sentinel Island stay safe?' (Textbook p. 98.) Students discuss in small groups and share ideas with the class. Teacher scribes key ideas on the board: what signs in nature might they have read?

Class reflects on the broader question: Where else do people read nature's signs to make decisions — fishermen reading clouds, farmers reading seasons, herders knowing animal behaviour? Students recall examples from their own families or communities and share them. Teacher connects these to the idea that long-lived knowledge of a place is a form of deep learning.

Students write one reflection sentence: 'One thing I can learn from the people of North Sentinel Island about living with nature is…' Teacher asks: 'What does this tell us about the relationship between people and the places they have lived in for a very long time?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how deep, long-held knowledge of a local environment equips a community to respond to natural events, and connect that principle to their own context.
periods.section_context: North Sentinel Island community, hunter-gatherer lifestyle, 2004 tsunami, reading nature signs for survival, indigenous ecological knowledge.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'What would you need to watch every day for months or years to know that something dangerous was coming?' This opens the idea that indigenous knowledge is built over generations, not from a single observation. Invite students to share any weather or season signs their grandparents or elders use.

periods.activity_title: Mangrove Forests — What Makes Them Unique
periods.textbook_anchor: Sundarbans: Home of the Mangroves — What do you find in the mangrove forest? List any three. (p. 99)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of Sundarbans mangrove forest and root structures on pp. 99–100

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Can you name a forest that grows in salty water?' Students guess freely. Teacher then introduces the Sundarbans and its location at the mouth of the Ganga. Students open Textbook p. 99 and look at the illustrations before reading.

Students read the section on mangroves (Textbook pp. 99–100) and list any three things found in a mangrove forest (Textbook p. 99). They then write their answer to 'What do you think makes this place different from other forests?' (Textbook p. 99). Students examine the textbook images of aerial roots and describe what they see in their notebooks.

Class shares observations. Teacher draws a simple diagram on the board showing muddy ground, waterlogged salty soil, and two types of root — aerial breathing roots and the spreading root network — labelling each. Students copy the diagram and add one label explaining each root's job.

Students write two observations: one about how aerial roots help the tree breathe, and one about how the root network helps the land. Teacher asks: 'If these roots were not there, what do you think would happen to the soil near the sea?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the structural features of a plant adapted to a waterlogged, saline habitat and explain the function of each feature.
periods.section_context: Sundarbans, largest mangrove forest, Ganga meets the sea, muddy and salty land, aerial breathing roots, root network holding soil, coastline protection.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Why can't most trees survive in salty, flooded soil?' This prompts them to think about what is special before they describe what they see. Encourage students to use the textbook images as their 'observation window' since they cannot visit the site.

periods.activity_title: People and the Mangrove — Generations of Dependence
periods.textbook_anchor: Sundarbans: Home of the Mangroves — In what ways do people in Sunderbans depend on the mangrove forests? (p. 100)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of Sundarbans community life and honey collectors on pp. 100–101

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to think about a forest they know — or have heard of — where people live and depend on trees. What do they take from the forest? Students share briefly. Teacher then focuses on the Sundarbans and the communities who live there.

Students read the relevant passage on Textbook pp. 100–101 about how people in the Sundarbans depend on the mangrove forest. They write their answer to 'In what ways do people in Sunderbans depend on the mangrove forests?' (Textbook p. 100). Students also look at the textbook image of honey collectors wearing tiger masks and discuss: 'Why do you think the honey collectors wear a mask on the back of their head?'

Class discussion: 'Why do you think it is important to take care of places like the Sundarbans?' (Textbook p. 101.) Teacher guides students to see that when the forest is healthy, the people who depend on it are also healthy — and vice versa. Students are invited to share examples of how their own community depends on a local natural feature: a river, a pond, a grove of trees.

Students write two sentences: one describing a way Sundarbans communities depend on the mangrove forest, and one explaining why protecting the forest also protects the people. Teacher asks: 'What do the honey collectors' masks tell us about how well these communities know the animals that share their forest?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a local community's way of life and the natural ecosystem they inhabit, and explain why protecting that ecosystem matters for the people within it.
periods.section_context: Sundarbans local communities, generational dependence on mangrove forest, honey collectors, tiger-mask tradition, mutual dependence of people and ecosystem.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students: 'The honey collectors have worn these masks for many generations — what does that tell you about how long people have lived alongside tigers here?' This surfaces the IKS dimension of long-held behavioural knowledge without labelling it. Accept diverse regional examples of community–nature links.

periods.activity_title: Northeast India — People, Animals, and Traditions
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Look at the picture. Identify three things being sold in the market. (p. 102)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook picture spreads of Northeast India — market, festival, stilt houses, wildlife on p. 102

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to close their books and imagine a region with lush forests, flowing rivers, bright festivals, and extraordinary wildlife. Students share any associations they have with Northeast India before opening the textbook.

Students open Textbook p. 102 and examine all the pictures on the page carefully before reading. They complete the four observation tasks: identify three things sold in the market, identify the festival in the picture, explain why houses are built on bamboo structures, name animals in the picture, and write what the pictures tell about people who live with nature (Textbook p. 102). Students record all responses in their notebooks.

Class shares observations section by section. Teacher adds information about the Seven Sisters states and Sikkim, Bhut Jolokia as a unique regional crop, and the region's biodiversity. Students update their notebook notes with any additional facts the class discussion surfaces.

Students write one sentence about something in the Northeast that surprised them from the pictures, and one sentence about how the stilt-house design shows the people's understanding of their environment. Teacher asks: 'What does the design of a house tell you about the land and weather where it was built?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe cultural and ecological diversity in a region by reading pictures, identifying specific features, and connecting physical environment to local practices.
periods.section_context: Northeast India Seven Sisters states and Sikkim, market goods, festivals, bamboo stilt houses, wildlife in pictures, Bhut Jolokia, lush forests and rivers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'Why might a house on bamboo stilts be better than a house on the ground in a region with heavy rainfall and flooding?' This connects architecture to ecology without lecturing. Encourage students to compare with house styles in their own region.

periods.activity_title: Hargila Conservation — Build a Bird's Nest
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Collect twigs, leaves and soft materials. Create a small bird's nest. What makes a good nest? (p. 104)
materials: small plastic egg or marble as stand-in for an egg
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of Hargila (Greater Adjutant Stork) and its nest on p. 104

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Hargila (Greater Adjutant Stork) and the community of women in Assam who teach children to protect the bird's nests. Students look at the textbook image (p. 104) and describe what they see in the nest — size, materials, location. Teacher asks: 'What would a nest need to keep eggs safe?'

In small groups, students collect the natural and paper materials available in the classroom and build a small bird's nest following the activity on Textbook p. 104. They weave, layer, and shape the materials. Each group places a small object (marble or paper ball) in the nest to test whether the egg stays in place.

Groups examine each other's nests and share: What did you use for the outer layer? What for the soft inner layer? Which nest held the 'egg' most securely? Teacher connects material choices to how real birds select materials — strength outside, softness inside — and to how the Hargila community's knowledge of nest locations helps them protect the birds.

Students write two observations in their notebook: one about what makes a nest strong and one about why people in the community choosing to protect nests matters for the bird's survival. Teacher asks: 'What would happen to the Hargila population if the nests were disturbed every breeding season?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can investigate the structural requirements of a natural shelter by building and testing a model, and connect community conservation behaviour to species survival.
periods.section_context: Hargila Greater Adjutant Stork, women-led community nest protection in Assam, bird nest construction using twigs, leaves, soft materials, egg safety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'If you were the bird, which part of the nest would you want to be strongest — the outside or the inside — and why?' This mirrors the inquiry the Assam community applies when choosing nest-protection strategies. Groups of three or four keep material sharing manageable.

periods.activity_title: Root Bridge Challenge — Engineering with Nature
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Connect two chairs using string or sticks in a way that will hold a small toy (p. 105)
materials: a small toy or eraser as the test load
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of living root bridges of Meghalaya on p. 105

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the textbook image of the living root bridges of Meghalaya (p. 105) and asks: 'How do you think people trained roots to grow like this? How long do you think it takes?' Students discuss the patience and deep knowledge of nature required. Teacher introduces the root bridge challenge.

In small groups, students attempt the root bridge challenge from Textbook p. 105: connect two chairs placed apart using string or sticks so the structure can hold a small toy placed on it. Groups may try more than one design. Each group tests their structure by placing the toy on it.

Groups share which designs held and which did not. Teacher asks: 'What made some bridges stronger — was it the material, the number of strings, or how they were arranged?' Students connect design choices to the way root bridges use many roots woven together for strength, rather than a single root.

Students write a one-sentence conclusion: 'The root bridge stays strong because…' Teacher asks: 'What does it mean that a bridge built from living roots gets stronger over time while a bridge built from wood or metal gradually weakens?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply engineering thinking to test how structural design choices affect the load-bearing capacity of a bridge model, and relate findings to a natural engineering solution.
periods.section_context: Living root bridges of Meghalaya, training roots across streams, bridge challenge with string and sticks between chairs, load-bearing test with small toy.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'The people of Meghalaya don't cut the roots — they guide them. How is guiding different from cutting, and why might that matter for how long the bridge lasts?' This keeps the inquiry connected to ecological thinking. Allow groups to try two designs if time permits before the share-out.

periods.activity_title: Local Conservation Plan — Protecting a Bird or Animal Near Us
periods.section_ref: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
periods.textbook_anchor: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions — Choose an animal or bird near you that needs protection. Create a protection plan and share it with the class. (p. 104)

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the Hargila conservation story and asks students to think of a bird, animal, or even an insect in their own neighbourhood, town, or region that they feel needs protection. Students think individually for a brief moment before sharing ideas with their group.

In small groups, students choose one local creature and create a short protection plan (Textbook p. 104). The plan includes: the name of the animal or bird, one threat it faces, two or three actions the group would take to protect it, and who they would involve. Groups record their plan in writing and add a drawing of the creature.

Groups share their protection plans with the class. After each presentation, the class offers one supportive suggestion. Teacher notes common themes: habitat protection, reducing human disturbance, community awareness. Teacher connects the groups' plans to the Hargila effort in Assam — ordinary people, local action, real outcomes.
Students write one sentence reflecting on what their plan would require of the people in their community: 'For our plan to work, the people around us would need to…'

periods.implied_lo: Students can create and present a community conservation plan for a local species, identifying threats and proposing specific protective actions.
periods.section_context: Local animal or bird needing protection, conservation plan including threats and actions, connection to Hargila community conservation model.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'Who in your community already knows the most about this animal — and how could you involve them in your plan?' This draws out the idea that elders, farmers, and local experts hold important ecological knowledge. Regionally varied choices of animal are all equally valid.

periods.activity_title: Western Ghats on the Map — Rivers, States, and Protected Areas
periods.textbook_anchor: Western Ghats — Look at the map, locate the Western Ghats and name the six states it passes through (p. 105)
materials: physical/political map of India (wall map or printed)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map of India showing the Western Ghats on p. 105

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: 'Can you trace a long chain of hills on a map of India running from north to south along the west coast?' Students look at the wall map and guess. Teacher reveals the Western Ghats and invites students to trace the range with their finger.

Students open Textbook p. 105 and locate the Western Ghats on the map. They name and record the six states the range passes through (Textbook p. 105). They then identify and write three rivers that originate from the Western Ghats (Textbook p. 106) and list three protected areas in the Western Ghats (Textbook p. 109).

Class compiles findings on the board. Teacher adds the endemic species mentioned in the section — lion-tailed macaque, Indian Giant Squirrel — and points to where they live on the map. Students note why a long north-to-south forested range would be a source of rivers flowing both east and west.

Students write two observations: one about the Western Ghats as a water source for the region, and one about why a forested mountain range would shelter more species than a cleared one. Teacher asks: 'What would happen to the rivers if the forests on the Ghats were removed?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate a natural geographic feature, identify the states it spans, and name rivers and protected areas associated with it.
periods.section_context: Western Ghats on map, six states the range passes through, rivers originating from Western Ghats, three protected areas, lion-tailed macaque, Indian Giant Squirrel.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why might a forested hill range be the birthplace of rivers rather than a bare rocky hill?' This encourages students to connect forest cover to water absorption and release — a systems idea — without giving them the answer directly.

periods.activity_title: Forest Peoples and Medicinal Plants of the Western Ghats
periods.textbook_anchor: Western Ghats — What are the people doing in the picture given below? (p. 106)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook pictures of tribal and forest-dwelling communities and medicinal plants on pp. 106–107

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to think of a time they or someone in their family used a plant or herb for health — a leaf, a root, a bark. Students share briefly. Teacher connects this to the communities of the Western Ghats who have developed deep knowledge of medicinal plants over generations.

Students open Textbook p. 106 and look at the pictures of people in the forest. They write their answer to 'What are the people doing in the picture?' (Textbook p. 106) and 'Why do you think forts were built on hilltops instead of flat land?' (Textbook p. 106). Students read the section content on tribal communities, forest food, and medicinal plants and take brief notes.

Class discussion: 'What would it mean for a community if the forest they have always depended on for food and medicine was destroyed?' Teacher guides students to see that losing a forest is also losing a library of knowledge built over generations. Students connect this to the Save Silent Valley Movement mentioned in the section — people who acted to prevent that loss.

Students write two sentences: one about what tribal and forest-dwelling communities know about the Western Ghats forest, and one about why that knowledge would be lost if the forest disappeared. Teacher asks: 'Who do you think knows most about a forest — someone who has studied it for a few years or someone whose family has lived in it for many generations?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a forest-dwelling community and their ecosystem, and explain how traditional knowledge of plants and resources is connected to the health of that ecosystem.
periods.section_context: Tribal and forest-dwelling communities of Western Ghats, traditional medicinal plants, forest food sources, hilltop forts, Save Silent Valley Movement.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'The textbook says these communities have lived in the forest for generations. What does that phrase tell you about the depth of their knowledge?' Encourage students to recall any elder in their own community who holds knowledge of local plants, seasons, or animals.

periods.activity_title: Fruit and Vegetable Variety Survey — Citizen Science in the Classroom
periods.textbook_anchor: Western Ghats — Pick a fruit or vegetable that grows in your state. Make a list of how many types and varieties are locally known. (p. 107)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustration of mango variety survey on p. 107

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the citizen-science mango survey described in the textbook (p. 107) where students, farmers, and experts worked together to count mango varieties. Students look at the textbook illustration and discuss: 'How many kinds of mango do you know by name?' Students share names and the teacher lists them on the board.

Students carry out the activity from Textbook p. 107: they choose a fruit or vegetable that grows in their state and, using their own knowledge and that of classmates, list as many local names, types, and varieties as they can find. Each student makes their own list in their notebook. The class then pools their lists on the board to create a combined class tally.

Class examines the combined tally. Teacher asks: 'Did we find more varieties than any one student knew alone? Why?' Students connect the idea of pooling knowledge to how the citizen-science survey worked — many people knowing different things together produce more complete knowledge. Teacher connects biodiversity of crop varieties to the biodiversity of the Western Ghats forest itself.

Students write one conclusion: 'We found that [crop name] has many varieties because…' and one reflection: 'What might be lost if only one variety of a crop was grown everywhere?' Teacher asks: 'Why might farmers have developed so many different varieties of the same fruit over hundreds of years?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a collaborative knowledge-gathering survey, pool individual findings to generate richer collective data, and connect crop biodiversity to the value of biological diversity more broadly.
periods.section_context: Citizen-science mango variety survey, local varieties of a chosen fruit or vegetable, collective classroom tally, biodiversity of Western Ghats crops.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Did your grandparents or older relatives know varieties that are harder to find today? What does that tell us?' This naturally surfaces the generational dimension of agricultural knowledge. Any locally familiar fruit or vegetable is equally valid — rice varieties, banana types, or leafy greens work as well as mango.

periods.activity_title: Aquatic Animals Match and Marine Biodiversity Consolidation
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Match the following aquatic animals with their features (p. 110)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook matching table of aquatic animals and features on p. 110

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to name as many sea creatures as they can from memory in one minute, then opens the discussion: 'What is special about each of these animals — how do they move, feed, or protect themselves?' Students share ideas freely.

Students open Textbook p. 110 and complete the matching exercise linking aquatic animals (dolphin, turtle, sea anemone, seahorse, clownfish, starfish, jellyfish, octopus) to their distinctive features. Students work individually first, then compare with a partner.

Class goes through the matches together. For each animal, teacher invites students to add one more observation: 'What else do you know about this animal? Where does it live in the sea?' Teacher connects back to the coral reef habitat explored in the Islands of India section — many of these animals live in or near reefs. Students correct and complete their matches.

Students write two sentences: one naming a marine animal and describing its special feature, and one explaining how the coral reef helps at least one of the animals in the matching list. Teacher asks: 'Which animal in the list surprised you most and why?'

periods.implied_lo: Students can match aquatic animals to their distinctive features and explain how a marine habitat structure supports the life of specific sea creatures.
periods.section_context: Dolphin, turtle, sea anemone, seahorse, clownfish, starfish, jellyfish, octopus; distinctive features of each; coral reef as habitat for marine animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask students: 'An octopus and a jellyfish both live in the sea, but they are very different from each other. What does that tell us about diversity in the ocean?' This consolidates the idea that one habitat can support many very different kinds of life.

periods.activity_title: Vibrant India Collage — Reflecting on People and Places
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Make a collage by pasting pictures depicting vibrant India (p. 111)
materials: Old magazines or printed images (pre-collected by students or provided by teacher)
plain paper or card for backing

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with three reflection prompts from Textbook p. 109: 'What surprised you most about the places visited in this journey across India?', 'Which place would you like to visit?' and 'How is your region similar to or different from one of the places in the chapter?' Students write brief individual responses in their notebooks before the collage work begins.

Students create their collage (Textbook p. 111) on a backing sheet, choosing images, drawings, or written labels that represent the four regions explored — islands, mangroves, Northeast India, Western Ghats — and the idea that people in each region live in harmony with nature. Students who do not have cut images draw and colour their own elements and paste them. Each student adds at least one short label explaining what their image shows.

Students do a brief gallery walk — placing their collages on desks and walking past each other's work. Each student notes one element from another student's collage that they had not included in their own. Teacher asks: 'What does it mean for a country to have so many different kinds of places and people?' Students share one or two responses aloud.

Students write a final sentence: 'One thing I will remember about India's unique places is…' Teacher closes by affirming that each of the four regions depends on its natural ecosystem — and on the people who know it well — to stay vibrant.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise learning about multiple regions by creating a visual representation that communicates the diversity of ecosystems and human-nature relationships across India.
periods.section_context: Collage depicting Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Sundarbans, Northeast India, Western Ghats; personal reflection on surprising features; comparison with own region; people living in harmony with nature.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If someone who had never visited India looked at your collage, what would they learn about the country?' This helps students think about what their choices communicate. Students who write rather than paste images should be equally encouraged — the output form matters less than the synthesis it demonstrates.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate and name natural geographic features using map symbols and spatial position.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Indira Point as southernmost tip of India, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Bay of Bengal, other Indian island groups visible on the map.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Look at the map for the southernmost point of India (p. 95)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students use a map of India to locate Indira Point and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, identify the surrounding sea, and record map observations in their notebooks.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple structural model to infer the engineering principle that a wider base increases the stability of a tall structure.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Paper-tube model without base support, triangular paper supports as buttress-root analogues, stability test on flat surface.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Islands of India — Roll newspaper into a tube, stand it up, add triangular supports, test stability (p. 96)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build a paper-tube model, test it with and without triangular base supports, and infer the structural principle underlying buttress roots.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the role of a natural habitat structure in sheltering living things and explain why aquatic ecosystems matter alongside land ecosystems.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Coral reefs, Marine Interpretation Centre, Andaman sea creatures including fish, marine invertebrates; parallel between reef shelter and forest shelter.

assessment_items.question_text: A student looks at a map of India and wants to find the southernmost tip of India. Which point should they look for on the map?

options.label: A
options.text: Indira Point

options.label: B
options.text: Kanyakumari

options.label: C
options.text: Lakshadweep

options.label: D
options.text: Rann of Kutch

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This tests direct map-reading recall from the textbook. Kanyakumari (B) is a common confusion as it is the southernmost tip of the Indian mainland but not of Indian territory overall — a student who selects this has not distinguished between mainland and island territories. Rann of Kutch (C) indicates a general confusion about Indian geography. Lakshadweep (D) indicates the student knows India has island territories but has confused the two island groups.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate and name natural geographic features using map symbols and spatial position.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses the southernmost point of the Indian mainland (Kanyakumari) with the southernmost point of Indian territory (Indira Point on the Andaman and Nicobar Islands), indicating incomplete map-reading of island territories.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has not used the map to locate India's southern extent and may be recalling a coastal name without spatial reasoning.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student knows India has island territories but has confused the Lakshadweep Islands (in the Arabian Sea, west coast) with the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (Bay of Bengal, southeast).

assessment_items.question_text: A student built a paper tube and stood it on a flat surface — it kept falling. Then they cut small triangles from thick paper and stuck them around the base. This time the tube stood upright. What does this activity show about how buttress roots help a tall forest tree?
expected_elements: The triangular paper supports spread the load outward at the base, increasing stability — just as buttress roots spread outward at the base of a tall tree.
Without supports (or buttress roots), a tall, narrow structure is easily toppled because the base is too small to balance the height.
The wider the base, the more stable the structure — this is the structural principle the activity demonstrates.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that name the wider base as the reason for stability and connect it explicitly to buttress roots. Award partial credit for responses that describe what happened in the activity correctly but do not make the connection to the tree root. Do not penalise students for not using the term 'buttress root' if the function is described correctly.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design and test a simple structural model to infer the engineering principle that a wider base increases the stability of a tall structure.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: The triangular supports spread the load at the base, making the structure stable — just as buttress roots spread outward around the base of a tall tree.
Without a wide base, a tall narrow structure (or tree trunk) tips over easily because the base cannot balance the height.
A wider base increases stability — this is the structural principle shown in the activity.

assessment_items.question_text: The Marine Interpretation Centre in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands shows visitors the coral reef. Which of the following best explains how the coral reef helps fish and other sea creatures?

options.label: A
options.text: The coral reef keeps the seawater warm so fish do not get cold.

options.label: B
options.text: The coral reef makes the sea deeper so large fish have more space.

options.label: C
options.text: The coral reef provides shelter, food, and a place to breed for many sea creatures.

options.label: D
options.text: The coral reef stops big waves from entering the sea.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This tests the student's understanding of the reef's ecological function as a habitat, drawn from the discussion in this section. Option B (warmth) reflects a common misconception about coral reefs as temperature regulators. Option C confuses the coastal protection role of mangrove roots (from another section of this chapter) with the reef's role. Option D introduces an unrelated idea about depth that has no basis in the section content.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the role of a natural habitat structure in sheltering living things and explain why aquatic ecosystems matter alongside land ecosystems.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has a misconception about coral reefs as temperature regulators, not recognising shelter, food, and breeding as the reef's primary ecological functions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has transferred the coastal protection role of mangrove root networks (from the Sundarbans section of this chapter) onto the coral reef, conflating the two distinct natural systems.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not engaged with the section content and is guessing based on a general sense that larger space helps fish, without understanding the reef as a specific shelter and food structure.

assessment_items.question_text: The people of North Sentinel Island have lived in the forest and near the sea for a very long time. Some people believe they knew something was about to happen before the 2004 tsunami struck. How do you think their long experience of living in their environment might have helped them? In your answer, explain what kinds of knowledge they might have used, and connect this to a way that people in your own community read nature's signs.
look_for: The student recognises that generations of close observation of nature — animals, sea, sky, wind — builds knowledge that cannot be gained quickly.
The student offers a plausible example of a nature sign the community might have read (animal behaviour, wave pattern, bird movement, unusual sounds) — not just a vague reference to 'knowing nature.'

The student connects this principle to a specific example from their own community (a farmer reading clouds, a fisherman reading wind, an elder knowing when rain is coming from plant or animal behaviour).
The student uses evaluative language — explaining WHY this kind of knowledge is valuable, not just stating THAT it is.
assessment_items.annotation: This is an open evaluative item; accept a wide range of specific nature signs and community examples — there is no single correct answer for the local connection. A strong response names both a plausible sign from North Sentinel Island AND a genuine example from the student's own context. A weak response only restates that the people 'know the forest' without naming specific signs or making the personal connection.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate how deep, long-held knowledge of a local environment equips a community to respond to natural events, and connect that principle to their own context.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Recognition that long-term, generational observation builds ecological knowledge that is difficult to acquire quickly.
A specific, plausible example of a nature sign the community might have read before the tsunami — animal movement, wave behaviour, unusual bird calls, changes in the sea.
A genuine personal or local connection: an elder, farmer, fisherman, or community member who uses nature signs in the student's own context.
Evaluative reasoning: the student explains WHY this knowledge is valuable, not only that it exists.

assessment_items.question_text: Mangrove trees grow in muddy, salty, waterlogged soil near the sea. Which of the following best explains how aerial (breathing) roots help mangrove trees survive in this habitat?

options.label: A
options.text: Aerial roots grow very deep into the soil to find fresh water below the salt water.

options.label: B
options.text: Aerial roots spread wide along the surface to stop waves from washing the tree away.

options.label: C
options.text: Aerial roots stick up above the waterlogged soil so the tree can take in air for breathing.

options.label: D
options.text: Aerial roots store extra salt from the soil so the rest of the tree stays healthy.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This tests the student's understanding of the specific function of aerial roots as described in the Sundarbans section. Option B confuses aerial roots with deep tap-root systems and misapplies the idea of freshwater-seeking. Option C describes the function of the spreading root network (soil-holding) rather than aerial roots, conflating the two types described in the section. Option D is a misconception not supported by the text — salt storage is not attributed to aerial roots in this section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe the structural features of a plant adapted to a waterlogged, saline habitat and explain the function of each feature.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has confused aerial roots with deep tap roots and has not understood that aerial roots project upward above the waterlogged soil to access air, not downward to access water.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has conflated the two root functions described in the section — they have assigned the soil-holding, coastline-protecting function (of the spreading root network) to the aerial roots instead.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student holds a misconception that aerial roots remove salt from the soil — a function not described in the section — possibly by analogy with how some plants handle toxins.

assessment_items.question_text: Honey collectors in the Sundarbans wear a mask on the back of their head when they go into the forest. They have done this for many generations. Explain why you think this practice developed, and what it tells us about the relationship between the people of the Sundarbans and the tigers that share their forest.
look_for: The student identifies that tigers in the Sundarbans attack from behind, and the mask on the back of the head deceives the tiger into thinking it is being watched.
The student explains this as a behavioural adaptation that protects honey collectors without harming tigers — a coexistence strategy rather than a conflict strategy.
The student reflects on the depth of observation required to develop such a practice — people who know tiger behaviour very well because they have shared the same forest for generations.
The student uses language that conveys a relationship of coexistence rather than one of dominance or fear alone.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that explain both the mechanism (masks fool the tiger) and the deeper insight (this is knowledge born of long coexistence). Accept student wording that conveys the same idea without using the term 'behavioural adaptation.' A response that only says 'to scare tigers' without explaining why it works is partial. Reward students who note that this practice protects both the collector AND does not require killing the tiger.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a local community's way of life and the natural ecosystem they inhabit, and explain why protecting that ecosystem matters for the people within it.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Identification of the mechanism: tigers attack from behind and the mask fools the tiger into thinking it is being watched from behind.
Recognition that this is a coexistence strategy — it protects the honey collector without requiring the tiger to be harmed or driven away.
Reflection on the depth of knowledge involved — this practice could only develop among people who have closely observed tiger behaviour over many generations.
Language that conveys a relationship of mutual presence in the forest rather than simple fear or dominance.

assessment_items.question_text: A student looking at pictures of Northeast India noticed that many houses are built on raised bamboo structures instead of directly on the ground. Give two reasons why this design suits the environment of Northeast India.
expected_elements: Northeast India receives very heavy rainfall, and raising the house on bamboo stilts protects it from flooding — water flows under the house rather than into it.
A raised structure also protects people and their belongings from animals and insects that move along the ground.
Bamboo is a local material that is strong, flexible, and grows abundantly in the region — using it shows how communities use what their environment provides.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any two well-explained reasons. The flooding / heavy-rainfall explanation and the bamboo-as-local-material explanation are the two most directly linked to the section. The animal-protection reason is also valid. Do not require all three — the task asks for two. Accept student phrasing that conveys the environmental logic clearly.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe cultural and ecological diversity in a region by reading pictures, identifying specific features, and connecting physical environment to local practices.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: Heavy rainfall and flooding in Northeast India make a raised floor essential — water flows under the house rather than into it.
Raised structures keep people and stored goods safe from ground-level animals and insects.
Bamboo is abundant, strong, and flexible — using local materials shows how the design fits the environment.

assessment_items.question_text: A group of students in Assam built a bird's nest from twigs, dry leaves, and cotton wool. When they placed a small marble inside, it rolled out of one nest but stayed safely in another. What did the group find out about what makes a good nest? Name two features of a good nest and explain why each feature matters.
expected_elements: A good nest has a firm, woven outer layer (made from stiff twigs or sticks) that holds the shape and prevents it from collapsing — this keeps the egg from falling.
A good nest has a soft inner layer (cotton, grass, feathers, or soft leaves) that cushions the egg and prevents it from cracking or rolling.
The nest should be shaped like a bowl or cup — a flat nest lets the egg roll away, while a curved base holds it in the centre.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any two features that are clearly explained in terms of why they matter for egg safety. The three expected elements are all valid — students need only name two. Reward responses that describe both the material and the structural reason, not just 'it was soft' or 'it had twigs.'
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can investigate the structural requirements of a natural shelter by building and testing a model, and connect community conservation behaviour to species survival.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: A firm, woven outer layer of stiff twigs holds the nest's shape so it does not collapse under the egg's weight.
A soft inner layer (cotton, grass, tissue) cushions the egg and prevents it from cracking or being damaged.
A bowl or cup shape keeps the egg from rolling out — a flat surface allows the egg to slide away.

assessment_items.question_text: Students tried the root bridge challenge: they connected two chairs using string and sticks to hold a small toy. Some designs held the toy and some did not. What does this activity tell us about why the living root bridges of Meghalaya are so strong? Name one design feature that made a bridge hold the toy, and explain how the same idea works in a living root bridge.
expected_elements: Using many strings or sticks woven together (rather than a single string) spreads the load across the structure — just as a living root bridge uses many roots growing together rather than a single root.
Anchoring the structure firmly at both ends (the chairs) before loading it prevents it from sagging or swinging — just as root bridges are anchored to living trees on both banks of the stream.
A taut, tight structure (no slack in the strings) distributes the weight more evenly — living root bridges grow tighter and stronger over time as more roots join the structure.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for any one design feature that is clearly explained and correctly connected to the living root bridge. Students may name different features from the three expected elements — any feature that accurately describes their own trial and is correctly applied to the root bridge principle is valid.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply engineering thinking to test how structural design choices affect the load-bearing capacity of a bridge model, and relate findings to a natural engineering solution.

competency.competency_text: Gains familiarity with using the scientific method in investigations, as well as familiarity with other crosscutting concepts such as energy, matter, and systems that apply across the domains of science and engineering

expected_elements: Using many strings/sticks together spreads the load — living root bridges use many interwoven roots rather than a single root for the same reason.
Anchoring firmly at both ends before loading prevents collapse — root bridges are anchored to living trees on both banks.
A taut, tight structure distributes weight evenly — living root bridges grow stronger over time as more roots weave in, increasing tautness and load capacity.

assessment_items.task: Think of a bird, animal, or insect that lives near your home, school, or neighbourhood and that you feel needs protection. Create a short Protection Plan for this creature. Your plan should include: (1) the name of the creature, (2) one main threat it faces, (3) two actions you and your community could take to protect it, and (4) a drawing of the creature in its habitat.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My creature: ___
One threat it faces: ___
Action 1 we can take: ___
Action 2 we can take: ___
Drawing of the creature in its habitat: [space for drawing]
format_of_output: Written protection plan (name, threat, two actions)
Drawing of the creature in its habitat
assessment_items.annotation: There is no single correct creature or set of actions — accept any locally known animal, bird, or insect and any culturally or ecologically appropriate protective actions. Regionally varied answers are acceptable and correct: a student in a coastal area naming a sea turtle, a student in a forest-edge community naming a specific bird, and a student in a city naming a sparrow or stray dog are all equally valid. Assess whether the threat is realistic and the actions are specific and doable — not whether the creature is 'important enough.'
assessment_items.chapter_section: Northeast India: Green Hills and Great Traditions
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can create and present a community conservation plan for a local species, identifying threats and proposing specific protective actions.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can identify a real threat to a local species, propose specific and realistic protective actions, and communicate their plan visually and in writing — demonstrating conservation thinking applied to their immediate environment.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold breaks the plan into four parts. Look for whether the threat is specific (not just 'people are bad to animals') and whether the two actions are genuinely doable by students and their community (planting trees, not disturbing nests, spreading awareness, keeping a local water source clean).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong plan names a specific local creature, identifies a precise and realistic threat, and proposes two actions that are concrete and community-connected. A weak plan names a vague or remote creature (a tiger in a distant forest) and suggests actions that are impractical for children or a local community.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw may describe the habitat in words. Students who know a creature in a regional language may name it in that language with a brief description. Students in urban settings are equally encouraged to name urban wildlife — sparrows, bats, monitor lizards.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The combination of written text and a drawing mirrors the Hargila conservation group's approach of both knowing the bird and being able to communicate that knowledge to others. The drawing anchors the creature in its habitat, not in isolation.

assessment_items.question_text: A student looks at a physical map of India and traces a long chain of forested hills running from north to south along the west coast. She names six states it passes through and notes that several major rivers begin here. Which natural feature is she identifying?

options.label: A
options.text: The Aravalli Hills

options.label: B
options.text: The Eastern Ghats

options.label: C
options.text: The Vindhya Range

options.label: D
options.text: The Western Ghats

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. This tests map-reading and recognition of the Western Ghats' key characteristics — west coast location, north-south orientation, six states, river origin — drawn directly from the map work in this section. Option B (Eastern Ghats) is a direct name confusion — students who have not read the map carefully may conflate the two. Option C (Vindhya Range) runs east-west across central India, not north-south along the coast. Option D (Aravalli Hills) runs through northwest India and is not associated with river origins or forest biodiversity in the way described.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a country-level map to locate a natural geographic feature, identify the states it spans, and name rivers and protected areas associated with it.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses the Western and Eastern Ghats — likely because both are hill ranges in peninsular India. The student has not used the west-coast position or the six-state count to distinguish between them.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student names a different Indian hill range without applying the map clues given in the question (west coast, north-south, river origins). This indicates general recall of hill range names without map-reading application.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student names another Indian hill range (Aravallis, in Rajasthan/Gujarat) without applying the geographic clues in the question, indicating confusion between Indian mountain ranges.

assessment_items.question_text: Tribal and forest-dwelling communities have lived in the Western Ghats for many generations and know its plants, animals, and seasons deeply. The Save Silent Valley Movement brought together these communities and others to protect the forest from a planned dam. Explain why protecting this forest mattered so much to the forest communities, and what would have been lost — for both people and nature — if the forest had been destroyed.
look_for: The student identifies that forest communities depended on the Western Ghats forest for food, medicine, and livelihood — not just as a scenic place but as the foundation of their way of life.
The student explains that the forest contains endemic species (animals, medicinal plants) found nowhere else — destroying it would mean permanent loss of these species.

The student articulates that the traditional knowledge of tribal communities about plant medicines and forest resources would also be lost along with the forest — knowledge cannot survive without the ecosystem it was built on.
The student makes an evaluative statement about why community-led conservation (the Save Silent Valley Movement) is significant — ordinary people, not just governments or experts, can protect nature.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that address both the human and ecological dimensions of the loss. A response that only describes the ecological loss (endemic species) without the human-cultural dimension (loss of livelihood, loss of traditional knowledge) is partial. Reward students who articulate that traditional knowledge disappears when the ecosystem it is tied to disappears — this is the most sophisticated insight available in the section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe the relationship between a forest-dwelling community and their ecosystem, and explain how traditional knowledge of plants and resources is connected to the health of that ecosystem.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

look_for: Recognition that forest communities depended on the Western Ghats for food, medicine, and livelihood — the forest is the foundation of their daily life, not just a background.
Understanding that the forest contains endemic species found nowhere else — their loss would be permanent and irreversible.

The insight that traditional knowledge of plants and forest resources cannot survive without the ecosystem it was built on — destroying the forest also destroys centuries of accumulated human knowledge.

An evaluative comment on the significance of community-led conservation — the Save Silent Valley Movement shows that ordinary people can and did protect a forest that governments or commercial interests might have sacrificed.

assessment_items.question_text: A class decided to find out how many varieties of a fruit or vegetable they could name together. Each student listed varieties they knew, then the class pooled all their lists. They found far more varieties together than any one student knew alone. What does this activity show about how knowledge about local crops can be gathered and why it matters?
expected_elements: Pooling individual knowledge produces a richer, more complete picture than any single person can provide — this is the principle of citizen science: many people contribute small pieces that together build a larger understanding.
The variety of names and types reflects real biodiversity — if many varieties of a crop exist, the ecosystem and the farming communities have maintained that diversity over many generations.
This kind of knowledge, held by farmers, elders, and community members, is valuable for conservation — knowing what varieties exist is the first step in protecting them.
assessment_items.annotation: Award full credit for responses that address both the method (pooling knowledge produces more than one person knows) and the significance (this knowledge reflects biodiversity worth protecting). A response that only describes what the class did without explaining why it matters is partial. The specific fruit or vegetable the student refers to may vary by region — all are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a collaborative knowledge-gathering survey, pool individual findings to generate richer collective data, and connect crop biodiversity to the value of biological diversity more broadly.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: Pooling each student's individual knowledge produces a richer, more complete list than any one person could create — this is the core principle of citizen science.
The number and variety of names reflects real biodiversity that farmers and communities have maintained over generations — many varieties means a healthy, diverse crop base.
Recording and sharing this knowledge is itself a conservation act — knowing what varieties exist is necessary before they can be protected or grown deliberately.

assessment_items.question_text: A student is completing a matching exercise on aquatic animals. She needs to match the seahorse to its most distinctive feature. Which feature should she select?

options.label: A
options.text: The male seahorse carries and protects the eggs in a pouch.

options.label: B
options.text: The seahorse can sting other animals with its tentacles.

options.label: C
options.text: The seahorse has a hard shell to protect its body.

options.label: D
options.text: The seahorse uses its eight arms to catch prey.

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Option B describes the octopus (eight arms), which is another animal in the matching exercise — a student selecting this has confused two animals from the same list. Option C describes a turtle or a crustacean — a student selecting this may be thinking of the word 'horse' and imagining armour. Option D describes a jellyfish or sea anemone — a student selecting this has confused the stinging feature with the seahorse.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can match aquatic animals to their distinctive features and explain how a marine habitat structure supports the life of specific sea creatures.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the seahorse with the octopus — both are in the matching exercise. This indicates the student completed the matching task but mixed up two animals from the same list.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student associates the word 'horse' with armour or hardness, or is thinking of a turtle's hard shell, indicating they have not read the seahorse's listed feature from the matching exercise.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused the seahorse with the jellyfish or sea anemone, which use stinging cells — a confusion between two marine animals from the same matching list.

assessment_items.task: Create a collage or a labelled drawing that shows vibrant India — including at least three of the four regions explored in this chapter (Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Sundarbans, Northeast India, Western Ghats). For each region you include, add a short label (one or two words or a sentence) that names something special about that region's nature OR its people. Below your collage, write two sentences: one about what surprised you most in this chapter, and one about how people in different regions live in harmony with nature.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Region 1: ___ [image or drawing] Label: ___
Region 2: ___ [image or drawing] Label: ___
Region 3: ___ [image or drawing] Label: ___
(Optional Region 4: ___ [image or drawing] Label: ___)
What surprised me most: ___
How people live in harmony with nature: ___
format_of_output: Collage or labelled drawing with at least three regions represented
Short label for each region naming something special
Two written sentences (one personal reflection, one about people-nature harmony)
assessment_items.annotation: There is no single correct visual output. Assess whether the student has represented at least three distinct regions, whether each label correctly names a feature of that region (not a generic statement), and whether the two sentences reflect genuine engagement with the chapter content. A collage made only of drawings is equally valid to one made of cut images. Students who write detailed labels and brief sentences may show stronger synthesis than students with elaborate visuals and vague labels — attend to the labels and sentences, not the artistic quality.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise learning about multiple regions by creating a visual representation that communicates the diversity of ecosystems and human-nature relationships across India.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can select and represent knowledge from multiple regions, communicate what is distinctive about each, and articulate a personal synthesis about India's diversity and the relationship between people and nature.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: Look for specificity in the labels — 'mangrove aerial roots hold soil' is stronger than 'forests.' The two sentences at the bottom are the clearest window into the student's synthesis: a student who can say what surprised them and WHY has moved beyond listing facts.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: A strong response covers at least three regions with specific, accurate labels and writes sentences that show genuine reflection. A weak response labels regions with only a region name and writes generic sentences like 'India has many forests and rivers.'
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot cut and paste may draw all elements. Students with limited written English may write labels in their home language with a brief translation. Students who include a fourth region should be acknowledged. The collage and the sentences are equally weighted — an outstanding written reflection with a simple drawing is as valid as an elaborate collage with thin writing.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Collage or labelled drawing plus two written sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The combination of visual and written output mirrors the chapter's dual strand — natural features (shown visually) and human-cultural responses (articulated in writing). The scaffold ensures all students engage with both modes regardless of artistic confidence.
